newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore office property sector set for long pause.
newsitem.headline: Singapore office property sector set for long pause.

text.p: Singapore office property prices and rents look set for a long pause after soaring by almost 80 percent in the last three years, analysts and property consultants said on Monday.
They said a slowing economy and new office space over the next two years would cap any major increases in rentals and capital values.
Real estate consultants Colliers Jardine said it expected an estimated 865,000 sq m (9,310,773 sq ft) of new office space to come on the market between 1996 to 1998.

"This supply is greater than that for the last three years of 635,000 sq m and it is coming onto the market at a time when economic growth and business conditions are expected to be slower," Colliers said in a September research report.
Singapore's rapid expansion is expected to slow, with gross domestic product growth of between 7.0-8.0 percent in 1996, after an 8.8 percent rise in 1995 and 10.1 percent in 1994.

Strong growth in the last couple of years was led mainly by the financial and manufacturing sectors. The expansion of financial institutions, in particular, contributed significantly to demand for office space.
"The financial sector has slowed down. Leasing activity has slowed in the last few months," said Lim Chung Chun, property investment analyst with ING Barings.
Lim, who recently recommended investors sell office property stocks, said he forecast a net absorption of about 204,000 sq m of office space in 1996, lower than last year's 209,000 sq m.
"I think the occupancy rate is likely to drop over the next 15 months. It is currently at 90.6 percent and I expect it to fall below 90 percent going into 1997."
Analysts said slowing rentals and capital values would be a welcome change as prices had risen too sharply.
"A slowdown is not necessarily bad as Singapore needs to remain competitive with other Asian cities," said Ong Choon Fah, director with real estate consultants Edmund Tie & Co.
She said in recent years Hong Kong office rents had come down while Singapore rents rose.
Colliers said prime office rents in Hong Kong were 189 percent higher than Singapore in 1993, but were now only 52 percent higher.

"There has been some resistance from tenants, especially multi-nationals, to higher rents in Singapore," said Ong. "Certainly we won't see the kind of rental growth we have seen in the last two years.".
The pause in rents would also be reflected in capital values of office buildings, expected to remain flat or rise marginally over the next 12 months, the analysts said.
Colliers said office space in central Raffles Place, now S$21,500 to S$25,800 psm, could see another five percent rise.
Analysts said that despite high prices, foreign and local investors continued to be interested in buying office space in Singapore.
Recent government land sales for commercial properties saw HongKong Land Holdings and Malaysia's Hicom Holdings submitting top bids.
